anomaly.observation: Three disjoint views of port 18080 disagreed at the same instant: (a) netstat -ano listed NO listening socket; (b) Get-NetTCPConnection listed NOTHING; (c) HTTP GET /props returned a valid llama.cpp payload with build_info=b1-88c4bc6 and model alias identity-copy.gguf.

evidence_for: HTTP GET /props on 127.0.0.1:18080 returns build_info=b1-88c4bc6 with model alias identity-copy.gguf, matching that binary path
process_attribution.not_verified: That PID 21612 actually holds the bound socket. Neither netstat -ano nor Get-NetTCPConnection named any owning process for 18080 at the same instant, so the socket owner was never directly confirmed.
process_attribution.statement: PID 21612 is the LEADING PROCESS CANDIDATE associated with port 18080.
process_attribution.wording_rule: Do not write 'confirmed to hold port 18080'. Write 'leading process candidate associated with port 18080' until a socket-owner view names it directly.

anomaly.resolution: PARTIALLY RESOLVED. Two llama-server processes exist (PID 4660 started 02:03:28, PID 21612 started 03:23:49). PID 21612's cmdline carries --port 18080 and /props answers with that instance's build. The epoch-1 boundary recorded PID 31800, which is GONE. So the process currently serving 18080 is NOT the one epoch 1 measured.
anomaly.why_netasm_and_getnettcpconnection_agree: UNDETERMINED but no longer load-bearing: the server is reachable and identifies itself. Both Windows socket queries returning empty while an HTTP endpoint on that exact port answers is consistent with a permissions/visibility limitation on socket enumeration, not with the port being free.

scope: Stored observer output and its revision; endpoint properties do not certify socket owner. No fresh server query or GPU/process control.
